transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-15
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55m
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Olivia Park (Head of ML - Sentinel), Carlos Mendes (Platform Eng), Asha Rao (Security Lead)

Summary: quick intro, goal is to scope POC for inference for Sentinel's customer-facing fraud scoring and explanations. Focus on workload sizing and benchmarks.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, then we want to understand your traffic shape and success criteria so we can scope a meaningful POC.
[00:22] Olivia: Thanks, Maya. Olivia here. high level, we run a retrieval + ranking + explain step for transaction review. the explain is a small LLM call that annotates flagged transactions. average 200 transactions per second in peak windows across pipelines but only a subset get explain calls, so rough target is 200 to 300 QPS for the LLM inference during peaks.
[00:45] Liam: okay great. do you have concurrency expectations? is that bursty or fairly steady?
[00:52] Carlos: it's very spiky. we see bursts on payroll days and end of month, like short 2-8 minute spikes where QPS jumps 3-4x. average concurrency for explain calls we measured is about 180 concurrent request contexts in those spikes.
[01:18] Maya: good, that helps. can you share average prompt sizes? input token distribution?
[01:26] Olivia: yeah, our sample shows median input tokens ~80, 75th 160, 95th about 420 when we include extra context details. output is usually short: median 40 tokens, 95th around 120. sometimes longer if we ask for a detailed justification.
[01:47] Liam: perfect. those numbers are exactly what we need to project compute. so baseline model you're considering for POC?
[01:55] Olivia: we were thinking of open models, but we want to test both hosted and a dedicated option. privacy wise, we need data not to persist in the public cloud logs, and Asha will talk requirements.
[02:10] Asha: right, SOC2 and SSO integration are must-haves. we need audit logs and KMS support for keys. also data residency in the EU for a subset of customers.
[02:27] Maya: totally understood. Redwood Dedicated or Private will cover VPC+KMS. hosted can be done with our SOC2 controls but we can discuss retention policies.
[02:38] Liam: on the perf side, with median input 80 and median output 40 tokens, and p95 output 120, we can estimate token per request around 200 tokens in worst case. with 250 QPS that's 50k tokens per second. for GPU sizing, that'll affect throughput significantly.
[02:58] Carlos: can you walk through the math? like how you convert tokens/sec to GPU utilization?
[03:05] Liam: sure. rough method: tokens/sec * tokens per GPU throughput depends on model and quantization. example, for a 13B quantized config on A100-like hardware we might get 10k-20k tokens/sec per GPU for streaming workloads depending on concurrency and batching. so at 50k tokens/sec we'd likely need 3-6 GPUs depending on model variant and whether KV cache reuse/prefix caching reduces average work.
[03:35] Olivia: okay and latency targets? we expect p95 <= 500ms for the explanation call, ideally p95 <= 300ms for short prompts.
[03:45] Maya: those are reasonable SLAs. success criteria let's write down: 1) p95 latency under 300ms for short prompts (input < 120 tokens), 2) throughput target to sustain 250 QPS with acceptable p95 under 500ms for mixed sizes, 3) accuracy/quality pass on a 200-sample eval set with metrics you define.
[04:08] Olivia: yes that's our ask. also cost per 1M requests budget threshold — we can share target, but ballpark we want to evaluate to see if dedicated setup gets us below hosted unit cost.
[04:18] Liam: noted. for benchmarking we'll run two configurations: hosted Redwood API with your traffic replay, and a Dedicated private cluster with similar model to compare latency and unit cost.
[04:31] Carlos: timeline wise, how long to spin a POC?
[04:35] Maya: typical POC is 3 weeks of active benchmark and integration work: week 1 set up and run baseline small tests, week 2 run full-scale load tests and iterate on config, week 3 analyze results and tune. we can compress if we get traces and prompt sets today.
[04:49] Olivia: sounds good. for the load test we can provide a traffic replay and a sandbox dataset. does Redwood need keys or real data?
[04:56] Asha: we will only provide anonymized traces for now. if dedicated Private, we can run behind their VPC and you can give us docker images or agent to run tests; but during hosted we'll only replay anonymized samples.
[05:12] Liam: that's fine. we often run a synthetic replay that mirrors your input token distribution — median/75/95 we asked for are perfect.
[05:21] Maya: quick question on reranking vs generation. you mentioned retrieval + ranking + explain. which stage is LLM heavy?
[05:29] Olivia: the explain step is generation for human-facing rationale. reranking is a short embedding/rerank which is less of an LLM throughput challenge but costs add up. for the POC we want to focus on explain generation.
[05:44] Liam: okay focusing on explain makes benchmarking simpler. we'll include a small rerank baseline to account for end-to-end latency.
[05:52] Carlos: about concurrency and batching — do you have suggestions for optimal batching window? our traffic is spiky and we need to keep tail latency low.
[06:01] Liam: yeah, for spiky workloads continuous batching with a small batching window (e.g., 10-20ms) can improve GPU utilization without hurting p95 too much. we can also apply prefix caching if many prompts share a common prompt header, that reduces repeated work.
[06:19] Olivia: we do have a lot of shared header context in the explain templates, so prefix caching could help.
[06:25] Liam: great. we'll try a workload config that leverages caching.
[06:28] Maya: switching to success metrics again. on quality, do you have an eval rubric?
[06:33] Olivia: we'll provide a 200-sample labeled set where responses are graded for relevance and factuality and a pass threshold of 85% weighted accuracy.
[06:43] Maya: perfect, we'll run automatic evals and manual spot checks.
[06:47] Liam: also, we should decide which model families to test. we can try a smaller 7-13B to hit latency targets and a 70B if you want higher quality. note larger models increase tokens/sec needs but may reduce number of calls due to higher quality — tradeoff to consider.
[07:06] Carlos: budget favors smaller models but we need to see if quality meets the 85% threshold. so compare 13B quantized vs 70B-quantized candidate.
[07:17] Olivia: can Redwood do quantization recommendations and automated pipeline?
[07:21] Liam: yes, Redwood Optimize recommends quant profiles per workload. we'll include recommended quantization levels in the report.
[07:29] Asha: security — SSO, SAML, and audit logs are needed. for Dedicated we need HSM/KMS integration for key management, and for hosted we need explicit log retention policies and PII redaction options.
[07:44] Maya: noted. we'll attach our security pack and SOC2 evidence. for KMS we support BYOK and HSM integrations on Dedicated/Private.
[07:54] Carlos: good. about data residency, some EU accounts can't cross borders. can we scope a POC limited to eu-west-1 region?
[08:02] Liam: yes, we can run dedicated instances in eu-west-1 or hosted with region pinning for those tenants. we'll document network and egress controls.
[08:12] Olivia: thanks. can you talk about failure modes and graceful degradation? if capacity spikes exceed thresholds how does Redwood fallback?
[08:20] Liam: we have smart routing and fallback policies. for example if dedicated capacity is saturated we can route to a lower-cost hosted variant or a smaller model with a quality flag. you can configure canary rollouts and automatic fallbacks.
[08:34] Maya: okay let's capture explicit POC acceptance criteria: 1) p95 latency for short prompts under 300ms, 2) sustain 250 QPS with p95 under 500ms for mixed sizes, 3) quality >= 85% on your eval set, 4) cost estimate per 1M requests and target delta between hosted/dedicated.
[08:56] Olivia: agreed.
[09:00] Liam: next on benchmarks: we'll want historical traces to generate a realistic replay. if you can't share raw data, a histogram of request sizes and timestamps is good too.
[09:11] Carlos: we can provide anonymized traces with fields: timestamp, prompt_length_tokens, response_expected_length and a label for customer region.
[09:21] Maya: perfect. once we have that we'll build a QPS model — show you expected GPU counts, per-token throughput, and cost estimates.
[09:30] Olivia: what about concurrency per user session? we often have bursty fan-outs where one event triggers 5 parallel explain calls.
[09:38] Liam: we can model fan-out by looking at per-event fan-out distribution. that affects concurrency but not total tokens/sec. we can generate scenarios: steady, burst, and extreme tail to measure p99 behaviors.
[09:51] Carlos: do you expose per-token billing or per-request billing?
[09:55] Maya: hosted is per-token + optional per-request for embeddings; Dedicated is committed capacity pricing + usage adjustments. we'll include sample math in the pricing sheet.
[10:05] Olivia: good. can Redwood run the test with our traces and return a report with latency percentiles, GPU utilization, and unit cost?
[10:12] Liam: yes that is standard. we'll run a hosted replay first, then dedicated cluster replay, and produce a benchmark report with configs, p50/p95/p99 latencies, token throughput, and cost per million.
[10:25] Maya: I'll send the benchmark template and pricing doc after the call.
[10:29] Olivia: great. question about throttling: if we exceed concurrency, what's the recommended policy? queue or shed?
[10:36] Liam: for customer-facing explain calls you'd probably prefer shed with graceful degraded responses rather than blocking. we can return cached short rationale or a fallback model. queueing increases latency which is bad for UX.
[10:48] Carlos: understood. for our POC we prefer a fallback to a smaller model with a quality flag.
[10:55] Liam: we can implement that in routing.
[11:00] Maya: quick operational ask — what logs/artifacts will we provide from the POC?
[11:05] Liam: the report will include latency percentiles, token counts, GPU metrics (utilization, memory), and request traces (anonymized). we'll also include recommended batch/window configs and quant profiles.
[11:18] Olivia: timeline recap?
[11:21] Maya: immediate: Maya sends docs and template by 2026-11-18. Sentinel shares traces by 2026-11-19. Redwood config and workload model 2026-11-20. Load test scheduled week of 2026-11-29. Results and tuning week of 2026-12-06.
[11:40] Carlos: ok that's workable.
[11:43] Asha: last note: we'll need an internal security review before any environment with production-level data; expect extra two weeks if that path chosen.
[11:53] Maya: noted. we'll treat POC as anonymized data phase first.
[12:00] Olivia: thanks all. next step for us is to collate the sample prompts and send them over.
[12:06] Maya: thanks team. we'll follow up with calendar invite for the load test and the docs.

End of transcript.

References and shared artifacts noted during call:
- Benchmark template (will be sent by Maya)
- Security pack and SOC2 evidence (attached link to security pack)
- Example config: redwood-dedicated-13b-quant (mentioned verbally, call transcript shows 'redwood-ded' typo sometimes)

Keywords occasionally mistranscribed: "Redwood Ded" for Redwood Dedicated, "KV cash" for KV cache, "A100-ish" as a shorthand for GPU class.
